text.p: These are the leading stories in the Belgrade press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Around 10,000 people attend rally in central Belgrade in support of teachers protesting over low and late wages. School strike dying down but schools still closed.
- Belgrade university students protest for 98th day, demanding resignation of rector.
- Italian parliamentary delegation to visit Belgrade March 9 to "express support for freedom and pluralism of information in Serbia".

- Losses of some socially-owned enterprises tripled in second half of 1996, while short-term credits doubled. Reduced export prices, high interest rates and unrealistic dinar exchange rate main reasons for increased losses, analysts say.
- Farmers demand cash for their products, rather than compensation which they say is detrimental to them.
- State is protecting debtors, rather than creditors, Jubanka director Marko Steljic tells annual assembly.
- Serbia's private businesses announce strike, demand restoration of recently abolished ministry of private enterprise.
- "Promises cannot be eaten," Zastava arms factory workers say, announce more protests over demands for wages and revival of production.
- Zastava Trucks to sign new agreement on cooperation with Iveco of Italy, which has a 46 percent stake in the Yugoslav factory. Zastava plans to produce around 1,300 trucks in 1997.
- Yugoslav Prime Minister Radoje Kontic continues consultations with parliamentary parties on make-up of new federal government.
- Debt to farmers for last year's crops to be repaid by March 15, farm exports to be subsidised, says Serbian Agriculture Minister Jovan Babovic.

- Serbian government team for construction industry says restructuring process to be speeded up, exports of goods and services to be stimulated, proposes that central bank issue guarantees to secure foreign investment.
- One of the biggest problems of Yugoslav banking sector is frozen hard currency savings. Without resolving this, there can be no new savings, says Privredna Banka Beograd director Milovan Kvrgic.
